question: How would you explain how Spring Security works to an interviewer?
title: How Spring Security Works — Complete Explanation for Interviews
direct_answer: Spring Security works through a filter chain that intercepts every HTTP request before it reaches your controllers. The filters handle: loading the SecurityContext, authenticating credentials, checking authorization, and handling exceptions. The SecurityContext stores the current user's Authentication throughout the request.

interviewer_intent.testing: High-level architectural understanding — the most common Spring Security interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only describing annotations without explaining the underlying filter chain
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a structured answer: filter chain → SecurityContext → Authentication object → authorization check

sections.title: Spring Security's Request Processing Architecture
sections.content: Spring Security is a **security framework** that protects your application by intercepting HTTP requests BEFORE they reach your controllers. Think of it as **airport security** — every passenger (request) must pass through multiple checkpoints (filters) before boarding (reaching the controller). The **filter chain** is the core: a sequence of 10-15 filters that examine the request. Key filters include: **UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter** (login), **BasicAuthenticationFilter** (HTTP Basic), **ExceptionTranslationFilter** (catches security errors), and **AuthorizationFilter** (checks permissions). Each filter decides: allow, deny, or pass to the next filter. The **SecurityContext** is a thread-local store holding the **Authentication** object (who you are + what roles you have). Once authenticated, every request can access `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` to know the current user. WHY filter chain? Separation of concerns — each filter does one job: parse JWT, load user, check roles, log audit trail.

sections.title: Basic SecurityFilterChain Configuration
Key Points
content: **Filter chain**: 10-15 filters execute in order before reaching your controller — each filter has a specific responsibility
**SecurityContext**: thread-local storage holding the Authentication object for the current request — cleared after response
**Authentication object**: contains principal (username), credentials (password), and authorities (roles/permissions)
**SecurityFilterChain bean**: replaces WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (deprecated) — defines URL rules and session policy
**SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS**: disables HTTP sessions — required for REST APIs using JWT tokens
**PasswordEncoder**: MUST be defined as a bean — BCryptPasswordEncoder is the standard choice for production
**Filter execution order**: cannot be changed arbitrarily — Spring Security orders filters by @Order values internally

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Spring Security protects your application using a filter chain that intercepts every HTTP request before it reaches your controller. Think of it like airport security — every request passes through multiple checkpoints. The core concept is the SecurityContext. It's a thread-local storage that holds the Authentication object for the current user. That object contains three things: the principal, that's the username, the credentials, that's usually the password, and the authorities, which are the roles or permissions. Here's how it works step by step. When a request arrives, the filter chain executes. First, filters check if there's existing authentication, maybe from a JWT token or a session cookie. If found, they load the Authentication into the SecurityContext. Next, the authorization filter checks if the user has permission to access the requested URL. If yes, the request continues to your controller. If no, Spring throws an AccessDeniedException, which returns a 403 Forbidden. One common mistake freshers make is thinking Spring Security is just about annotations like at-PreAuthorize. That's only the surface. The real power is the filter chain underneath. Every secured request goes through this chain, whether you use annotations or not. In production REST APIs, you'd configure a SecurityFilterChain bean. You set session policy to STATELESS, meaning no HTTP sessions. You disable CSRF because REST clients don't use cookies. You define URL rules using requestMatchers, like allowing slash-api-slash-public to everyone but requiring ADMIN role for slash-api-slash-admin. You also need a PasswordEncoder bean, usually BCryptPasswordEncoder, to hash passwords securely. To stand out in an interview, explain it in layers. Start with the filter chain concept. Then explain SecurityContext and Authentication. Finally, mention practical config like STATELESS session policy and PasswordEncoder. Show you understand both the architecture and the implementation.

seo.metaTitle: How Spring Security Works — Complete Interview Answer
seo.metaDescription: Complete explanation of how Spring Security works — filter chain, SecurityContext, authentication flow, authorization, 401 vs 403 for Java fresher interviews.

speakable_v2.hook: Spring Security is asked in nearly every Java backend interview — and the candidates who stand out can explain the filter chain architecture, not just the annotations on top of it.

beats.content: Spring Security works at the Servlet filter level. Every HTTP request passes through a chain of filters before it ever reaches your DispatcherServlet or controllers. Security is enforced before your code runs.

The filters have defined responsibilities in order. SecurityContextPersistenceFilter loads any existing authentication from the session. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter handles form login. For JWT-based APIs, your custom filter validates the JWT and populates the SecurityContext. ExceptionTranslationFilter converts security exceptions to 401 or 403 HTTP responses. The final AuthorizationFilter checks whether the current user's roles allow access to the requested URL.

When authentication succeeds — whether through form login or JWT — Spring creates an Authentication object with the user's identity and roles and stores it in a thread-local SecurityContext. Any code in that request can read the current user from there.
You configure all of this through a SecurityFilterChain bean. URL access rules, which auth mechanisms are active, CSRF settings, session management — all defined there.

speakable_v2.cap: Filter chain runs before controllers. Authentication sets the SecurityContext. Authorization checks the SecurityContext against URL rules. That's the full architectural loop.

question: How do you secure REST APIs using Spring Security?
title: Securing REST APIs with Spring Security — JWT Best Practices
direct_answer: Secure REST APIs with: stateless SecurityFilterChain (STATELESS session, CSRF disabled), JWT authentication (custom filter validates JWT per request), URL-based rules (requestMatchers), and optionally method-level security (at-PreAuthorize) for fine-grained data access control.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using form login for REST APIs — wrong approach, returns redirect HTML responses instead of JSON
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a complete answer: stateless + JWT + URL rules + method security + PasswordEncoder + exception handling

sections.title: REST API Security Architecture with Spring Security
sections.content: Securing REST APIs differs fundamentally from securing traditional web apps. REST APIs are **stateless** — each request must carry full authentication info (no server-side sessions). The solution: **JWT tokens**. The client sends credentials once to `/auth/login`, receives a JWT token, then includes that token in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header for every subsequent request. Spring Security's role: intercept requests, validate the JWT, extract user info, populate the SecurityContext, and enforce authorization rules. Key components: **(1) JwtAuthenticationFilter** — custom filter that validates JWT and sets Authentication, **(2) SecurityFilterChain** — configures STATELESS session, disables CSRF, defines URL rules, **(3) AuthenticationEntryPoint** — returns JSON 401 for invalid tokens (not HTML redirects), **(4) PasswordEncoder** — hashes passwords in the database. WHY disable CSRF? CSRF tokens protect cookie-based auth. REST APIs use bearer tokens, not cookies, so CSRF is irrelevant. WHY STATELESS? No HTTP sessions means horizontal scaling is trivial — any server can handle any request.

sections.title: Complete REST API SecurityFilterChain with JWT
Key Points
content: **SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS**: mandatory for REST APIs — no HTTP sessions, JWT carries all auth info per request
**CSRF disabled**: REST APIs use bearer tokens, not cookies — CSRF protection is unnecessary and breaks token-based auth
**JwtAuthenticationFilter**: custom filter (extends OncePerRequestFilter) validates JWT and populates SecurityContext on every request
**addFilterBefore()**: registers JWT filter BEFORE UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter — ensures JWT validation happens first
**AuthenticationEntryPoint**: returns JSON 401 for unauthenticated requests — default Spring behavior returns HTML redirect
**@EnableMethodSecurity**: required for @PreAuthorize annotations — replaces deprecated @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6
**Bearer token format**: client sends 'Authorization: Bearer <jwt>' header — filter extracts token, validates signature, checks expiry

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Securing REST APIs with Spring Security requires a stateless architecture. That means no HTTP sessions. Instead, you use JWT tokens. Here's the full flow. The client sends a POST to slash-auth-slash-login with username and password. Your login controller validates credentials using AuthenticationManager. If valid, you generate a JWT token containing the user ID and roles, sign it with a secret key, and return it in the response body. The client stores this token, usually in memory or local storage. For every subsequent request, the client includes the token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme. That's where Spring Security comes in. You create a custom JwtAuthenticationFilter that extends OncePerRequestFilter. This filter extracts the token from the header, validates the signature, checks if it's expired, and extracts user details. If valid, it creates an Authentication object and sets it in the SecurityContext. Then your controller methods can access the current user. In your SecurityFilterChain config, you must do four things. First, disable CSRF using csrf-dot-disable. CSRF tokens protect cookie-based sessions, but REST APIs don't use cookies. Second, set session management to STATELESS. This tells Spring not to create HTTP sessions. Third, define URL rules with requestMatchers. Allow slash-auth-slash-login and slash-auth-slash-register without authentication. Require specific roles for admin endpoints. Require authentication for everything else. Fourth, add your JWT filter before the UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter using addFilterBefore. One critical mistake freshers make is forgetting exception handling. By default, Spring Security returns HTML redirect responses for 401 and 403 errors. REST clients expect JSON. So you implement AuthenticationEntryPoint to return a JSON 401 for unauthenticated requests. You configure this in the exceptionHandling section of your SecurityFilterChain. For method-level security, add at-EnableMethodSecurity at the class level. This lets you use at-PreAuthorize on controller methods for fine-grained checks. For example, at-PreAuthorize with has-Role-ADMIN restricts a method to admins only. To stand out, mention the complete picture: STATELESS session, CSRF disabled, JWT filter before authentication filter, JSON exception responses, PasswordEncoder for hashing, and method security for role checks. Show you've thought through production concerns, not just hello-world tutorials.

question: What is the difference between stateless and stateful Spring Security?
title: Stateless vs Stateful Spring Security — REST vs Web App
direct_answer: Stateful Spring Security stores the Authentication in the HTTP session — the JSESSIONID cookie re-loads it per request. Stateless (STATELESS session policy) creates NO session — the Authentication is rebuilt from the JWT token on every request. REST APIs use stateless; traditional web apps use stateful.

interviewer_intent.testing: Architecture understanding of Spring Security modes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that stateless requires the SecurityContext to be populated per request by the JWT filter
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that in stateless mode, JWT filter must populate SecurityContext on EVERY request

sections.title: Session Management Strategies in Spring Security
sections.content: Spring Security supports two fundamentally different approaches to maintaining user authentication across requests: **stateful** (session-based) and **stateless** (token-based). In **stateful mode**, after successful login, Spring Security stores the `Authentication` object in the **HTTP session** on the server. The client receives a `JSESSIONID` cookie. On each subsequent request, the `SecurityContextPersistenceFilter` reads the session ID from the cookie, retrieves the stored `Authentication` from the session, and loads it into the `SecurityContext`. This is how traditional web applications work — think JSP, Thymeleaf, or any server-rendered UI. In **stateless mode** (`SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS`), Spring creates **NO HTTP session**. The `Authentication` is never stored on the server. Instead, each request must carry full authentication info — typically a **JWT token** in the `Authorization` header. A custom filter (like `JwtAuthenticationFilter`) extracts the token, validates it, and **rebuilds** the `Authentication` object from scratch on EVERY request. WHY stateless for REST? Horizontal scaling. Any server can handle any request without session replication.

sections.title: When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content: **Use stateful (session-based) security** when you're building traditional server-rendered web applications with JSP, Thymeleaf, or FreeMarker templates. These apps serve HTML directly and use form-based login with cookies. Session management is simpler here — Spring handles everything. Use it when you have a single monolithic server or can configure session clustering (Redis, Hazelcast). Also use stateful when you need server-side session features like remember-me, concurrent session control (max one login per user), or server-triggered logout. **Use stateless (token-based) security** when you're building REST APIs consumed by mobile apps, SPAs (React, Angular), or microservices. Stateless is mandatory for distributed systems where horizontal scaling is critical. Use it when you want zero server-side state — no session memory, no session replication complexity. Use it when your authentication info can be securely encoded in a JWT (user ID, roles, expiry). Use it when you need cross-domain authentication — JWT works across different origins, sessions don't without complex CORS cookie setup.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Stateful mode**: Authentication stored in HTTP session — SecurityContextPersistenceFilter loads it from session per request
**Stateless mode**: NO session created — JWT filter rebuilds Authentication from token on EVERY request
**JSESSIONID cookie**: identifies the session in stateful mode — sent automatically by browser on every request
**SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS**: disables session creation entirely — even calling request.getSession() returns null
**JWT filter responsibility**: in stateless mode, JWT filter MUST populate SecurityContext — if it fails, SecurityContext remains empty
**SecurityContext clearing**: Spring clears SecurityContext after each request in BOTH modes — thread safety guarantee
**Scaling implications**: stateless scales horizontally with zero config — stateful requires sticky sessions or Redis session replication

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between stateful and stateless Spring Security is all about where the authentication information lives between requests. In stateful mode, which is the default, Spring Security stores your Authentication object in the HTTP session on the server. After you log in successfully, Spring saves your user details in memory on the server. The browser receives a JSESSIONID cookie. On every subsequent request, the browser sends that cookie automatically. Spring's SecurityContextPersistenceFilter reads the session ID, retrieves your Authentication from the session, and loads it into the SecurityContext. You don't need to send credentials again. This works great for traditional web apps with server-rendered pages like JSP or Thymeleaf. In stateless mode, which you set using SessionCreationPolicy-dot-STATELESS, Spring creates NO session at all. Nothing is stored on the server. Instead, the client must send full authentication info with every single request, usually as a JWT token in the Authorization header. Here's the key difference. In stateless mode, a custom filter, typically called JwtAuthenticationFilter, runs on EVERY request. It extracts the token from the header, validates the signature, checks if it's expired, and rebuilds the Authentication object from scratch. Then it sets that Authentication in the SecurityContext. This happens on every single request. If the JWT filter fails or doesn't run, the SecurityContext stays empty, and you get a 401 error. One mistake freshers make is thinking stateless means no authentication. That's wrong. Stateless means no server-side session storage. You still authenticate, just differently. The JWT carries all the info needed to authenticate you on every request. Why choose stateless for REST APIs? Horizontal scaling. With no sessions, any server can handle any request. You don't need sticky sessions or Redis session replication. Every request is self-contained. That's huge in microservices or cloud deployments. Why choose stateful for web apps? Simplicity. Spring handles everything. You don't need to manage JWT tokens, expiry, refresh logic. You just use form login and cookies, and it works. To stand out, explain that in stateless mode, the JWT filter must populate the SecurityContext on EVERY request. Many freshers don't realize that. They think setting STATELESS is enough. It's not. You need a working JWT filter, or nothing works.

seo.metaTitle: Stateless vs Stateful Spring Security | Java Fresher Interview
seo.metaDescription: Compare stateless and stateful Spring Security — JWT vs session-based, STATELESS policy, SecurityContext lifecycle, horizontal scaling implications.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: Stateless and stateful Spring Security look similar to configure but have a completely different lifecycle for the SecurityContext — and the JWT filter's behavior depends entirely on which mode you're in.

beats.content: In stateful mode, after a successful login, Spring stores the Authentication in an HTTP session. Every subsequent request arrives with a JSESSIONID cookie, Spring loads the session, and the SecurityContext is restored with the user's Authentication. The user stays logged in across requests.

In stateless mode with SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS, Spring never creates a session. The SecurityContext starts completely empty on every single request. Your JWT filter is responsible for rebuilding it — it reads the token, validates it, loads the UserDetails, and sets the Authentication. After the request completes, the context is cleared. Next request starts fresh.

sharp edge: in stateless mode, if your JWT filter fails to set the SecurityContext for any reason — expired token, missing header, validation error — the request continues with an empty context and hits the authorization check as unauthenticated. This is correct behavior, but it means your filter must handle all JWT error cases gracefully and return 401 rather than letting the request continue.

speakable_v2.cap: Stateful: session restores the SecurityContext automatically. Stateless: JWT filter rebuilds it from scratch on every request. There is no persistence between requests in stateless mode.
followup_handoff: SessionCreationPolicy has other values besides STATELESS and IF_REQUIRED — ALWAYS and NEVER have specific use cases.
The SecurityContext clearing at end of request is handled by SecurityContextPersistenceFilter — understanding that filter explains the lifecycle.

question: How do you handle Spring Security exceptions in a REST API?
title: Spring Security Exception Handling for REST APIs — 401 and 403 JSON Responses
direct_answer: Implement AuthenticationEntryPoint to return JSON 401 for unauthenticated requests (instead of redirect). Implement AccessDeniedHandler to return JSON 403 for unauthorized requests. Configure them in the SecurityFilterChain with exceptionHandling().

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical REST security — returning proper JSON errors vs HTML redirects
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Spring Security returns HTML redirects for 401/403 by default — REST clients can't handle this
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler implementations

sections.title: Exception Handling in REST API Security
sections.content: By default, Spring Security is designed for **server-rendered web apps** — when authentication fails, it redirects to a login page (HTML response). When authorization fails, it redirects to an access-denied page. This breaks REST APIs. Mobile apps and SPAs expect **JSON responses** with proper HTTP status codes, not HTML redirects. The solution: implement two custom exception handlers. **AuthenticationEntryPoint** handles **authentication failures** — cases where the user is NOT authenticated at all (no token, invalid token, expired token). It should return a **401 Unauthorized** JSON response. **AccessDeniedHandler** handles **authorization failures** — cases where the user IS authenticated but lacks permission (wrong role). It should return a **403 Forbidden** JSON response. WHY two handlers? Different failure reasons need different status codes. 401 means "who are you?" — client should re-authenticate. 403 means "I know who you are, but you can't do this" — re-authenticating won't help. Spring Security's **ExceptionTranslationFilter** catches security exceptions and delegates to these handlers. You configure them in the `exceptionHandling()` section of your `SecurityFilterChain`.

sections.title: Custom Exception Handlers for REST API
Key Points
content: **AuthenticationEntryPoint**: handles unauthenticated requests — returns 401 JSON instead of HTML redirect to login page
**AccessDeniedHandler**: handles unauthorized requests — returns 403 JSON instead of HTML access denied page
**ExceptionTranslationFilter**: Spring filter that catches AuthenticationException and AccessDeniedException, delegates to configured handlers
**401 vs 403**: 401 means no valid authentication (client should retry with credentials), 403 means authenticated but insufficient permissions
**Default behavior**: Spring Security redirects to /login for 401 and /access-denied for 403 — breaks REST API clients expecting JSON
**ObjectMapper**: Jackson library for JSON serialization — inject as bean or create new instance for simple error responses
**exceptionHandling() config**: both handlers configured in SecurityFilterChain — authenticationEntryPoint and accessDeniedHandler methods

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Handling Spring Security exceptions in REST APIs is critical because the default behavior breaks REST clients. By default, Spring Security is designed for traditional web apps. When authentication fails, it returns an HTTP 302 redirect to slash-login. When authorization fails, it redirects to slash-access-denied. Both return HTML. A mobile app or React frontend can't handle HTML redirects. They expect JSON responses with proper status codes. The solution is two custom exception handlers. First is AuthenticationEntryPoint. This handles cases where the user is NOT authenticated. Maybe they didn't send a token, or the token is invalid or expired. You implement the commence method. Inside, you set the response status to 401, set content type to application-slash-json, and write a JSON error message. You include the error type, a message, and the request path. That's what the client needs to show a meaningful error. Second is AccessDeniedHandler. This handles cases where the user IS authenticated but doesn't have permission. Like a regular user trying to access an admin endpoint. You implement the handle method. Set status to 403, set content type to JSON, write an error response. The difference between 401 and 403 is important. 401 means "I don't know who you are, please authenticate." The client should prompt for login or refresh the token. 403 means "I know who you are, but you're not allowed to do this." Re-authenticating won't help. They need a different role. How do you wire these up? In your SecurityFilterChain configuration, there's a section called exceptionHandling. You call authenticationEntryPoint and pass your custom AuthenticationEntryPoint bean. You call accessDeniedHandler and pass your custom AccessDeniedHandler bean. Spring's ExceptionTranslationFilter, which is part of the default filter chain, catches security exceptions and delegates to these handlers automatically. One mistake freshers make is only handling AuthenticationEntryPoint and forgetting AccessDeniedHandler. If you have role-based security using has-Role or at-PreAuthorize, you MUST handle both. Otherwise, 403 errors still return HTML. Another mistake is using RestControllerAdvice with at-ExceptionHandler for security exceptions. That won't work. Security exceptions are thrown BEFORE reaching your controller, so controller advice never sees them. You must use AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler. To stand out, show both handlers in your answer. Explain the difference between 401 and 403. Mention that Spring's default behavior is HTML redirects, which breaks REST. Show you understand WHERE these exceptions are caught, in the ExceptionTranslationFilter, not in controller advice.

seo.metaTitle: Spring Security Exception Handling for REST APIs | Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn how to handle 401 and 403 as JSON responses in Spring Security REST APIs — AuthenticationEntryPoint, AccessDeniedHandler, exceptionHandling configuration.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API with JWT-based authentication
speakable_v2.hook: By default, Spring Security sends HTML redirects when auth fails — which looks fine in a browser but completely breaks any REST API client expecting JSON.

beats.content: Spring Security has two separate interfaces for the two different failure cases. AuthenticationEntryPoint handles the 401 case — the request has no valid authentication. That includes a missing token, an expired JWT, or an invalid signature. AccessDeniedHandler handles the 403 case — the user is authenticated but their roles don't grant access to the requested resource.

You implement both interfaces by writing directly to the HttpServletResponse: set the content type to JSON, set the appropriate status code, and write a JSON error body. Then you register both in your SecurityFilterChain with the exceptionHandling() DSL.

candidates miss: @ControllerAdvice cannot catch Spring Security exceptions. Those exceptions are thrown in the filter chain — before DispatcherServlet, before your controllers. @ControllerAdvice only handles exceptions that reach the DispatcherServlet. AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler are the only way to handle security exceptions with custom responses.

speakable_v2.cap: Implement AuthenticationEntryPoint for 401 JSON, AccessDeniedHandler for 403 JSON, register both in exceptionHandling(). @ControllerAdvice can't do this — security exceptions live in the filter layer.
followup_handoff: CORS headers must be present on 401 responses too — if they're missing, the browser blocks the error response and your frontend sees a CORS error instead of a 401.

sections.title: Core Spring Security Interview Topics for Freshers
sections.content: Spring Security interviews for freshers focus on **foundational concepts** and **practical REST API security**. Interviewers want to see: (1) architectural understanding (filter chain, SecurityContext), (2) hands-on config (SecurityFilterChain bean), (3) real-world patterns (JWT authentication, stateless sessions), and (4) problem-solving (exception handling, role-based access). The most asked question: **"How does Spring Security work?"** — tests whether you understand the filter chain architecture. Second most common: **"How do you secure REST APIs?"** — tests practical JWT implementation. Other frequent topics: **UserDetails vs UserDetailsService** (user loading), **authentication vs authorization** (who you are vs what you can do), **PasswordEncoder** (why BCrypt), **CSRF** (why disable for REST), **method security** (at-PreAuthorize), and **HTTP status codes** (401 vs 403). WHY these topics? They cover end-to-end security: loading users, verifying credentials, managing sessions, enforcing rules, and handling errors. Freshers often memorize syntax without grasping WHY. Interviewers probe: "Why disable CSRF?" "Why STATELESS?" "What happens if you don't configure PasswordEncoder?" Know the reasoning.

sections.title: Complete SecurityFilterChain Covering Key Interview Topics
Key Points
content: **Filter chain architecture**: most important concept — explain how requests pass through 10-15 filters before reaching controller
**Authentication vs Authorization**: authentication is WHO you are (login), authorization is WHAT you can do (permissions)
**UserDetailsService**: interface to load user from database — implement loadUserByUsername, return UserDetails object
**JWT flow**: client sends credentials → server validates → server returns JWT → client sends JWT in header → server validates per request
**SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS**: mandatory for REST APIs — no HTTP sessions, JWT carries all auth info
**PasswordEncoder**: MUST be configured as bean — BCryptPasswordEncoder uses salted hashing, resistant to rainbow table attacks
**CSRF disable for REST**: CSRF tokens protect cookie-based auth — REST uses bearer tokens, CSRF is unnecessary
**@PreAuthorize**: method-level security annotation — requires @EnableMethodSecurity, evaluated before method execution
**401 vs 403**: 401 = unauthenticated (no valid token), 403 = authenticated but unauthorized (wrong role)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: For Spring Security fresher interviews, you need to cover nine key topics. First, authentication versus authorization. Authentication is proving who you are, like showing your ID at an airport. Authorization is proving what you're allowed to do, like checking if your ticket is business class. In Spring Security, authentication happens first through filters like UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter. Authorization happens later through the AuthorizationFilter, which checks your roles against the required permissions. Second, how Spring Security works. This is the most common question. The answer is filter chain. Spring Security uses 10 to 15 filters that execute in sequence before your controller runs. Key filters include SecurityContextPersistenceFilter, which loads authentication from the session, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, which handles login, and AuthorizationFilter, which checks permissions. The SecurityContext holds your Authentication object throughout the request. Third, UserDetails and UserDetailsService. UserDetails is an interface representing a user. It has methods like getUsername, getPassword, and getAuthorities. UserDetailsService is an interface with one method: loadUserByUsername. You implement this to load users from your database. Spring calls it during login to verify credentials. Fourth, JWT authentication flow. The client posts credentials to slash-auth-slash-login. Your controller validates them using AuthenticationManager. If valid, you generate a JWT containing user ID and roles, sign it with a secret key, and return it. The client stores the token and sends it in the Authorization Bearer header for every request. A custom JWT filter validates the token and populates the SecurityContext. Fifth, SecurityFilterChain configuration. This bean replaced WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter. You define URL rules with requestMatchers, set session policy to STATELESS for REST APIs, disable CSRF, and add custom filters. Sixth, PasswordEncoder. You MUST configure this as a bean. Use BCryptPasswordEncoder in production. It uses salted hashing, which means even identical passwords produce different hashes. This defeats rainbow table attacks. If you don't configure a PasswordEncoder, Spring throws an error on startup. Seventh, CSRF. For REST APIs, you disable CSRF with csrf-dot-disable. CSRF tokens protect against cross-site request forgery in cookie-based authentication. REST APIs use bearer tokens in headers, not cookies, so CSRF doesn't apply. Eighth, method-level security using at-PreAuthorize. This annotation goes on controller methods to enforce role checks. For example, at-PreAuthorize with has-Role-ADMIN restricts a method to admins. You must enable this with at-EnableMethodSecurity at the configuration class level. Ninth, exception handling. Spring Security returns HTML redirects for 401 and 403 by default. REST clients need JSON. Implement AuthenticationEntryPoint for 401 and AccessDeniedHandler for 403. Configure them in exceptionHandling. 401 means unauthenticated, the client should retry with credentials. 403 means authenticated but unauthorized, you lack the required role. The key to standing out is explaining the WHY, not just the WHAT. Interviewers ask follow-ups like "Why disable CSRF?" or "Why STATELESS?" If you only memorize syntax, you'll struggle. Understand the reasoning. CSRF is disabled because REST uses tokens, not cookies. STATELESS is used because REST APIs scale horizontally without session replication. BCrypt is slow by design to resist brute-force. These are the answers that show depth.

question: What is the difference between Spring Security's @EnableWebSecurity and @EnableMethodSecurity?
title: @EnableWebSecurity vs @EnableMethodSecurity in Spring Security
direct_answer: at-EnableWebSecurity activates Spring Security's URL and filter-based security (SecurityFilterChain, request matching). at-EnableMethodSecurity activates method-level security annotations (at-PreAuthorize, at-PostAuthorize, at-Secured). Both are often used together for complete security coverage.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of the two security activation annotations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @PreAuthorize without @EnableMethodSecurity — annotation is silently ignored
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @EnableMethodSecurity replaced @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6

sections.title: Two Layers of Spring Security Activation
sections.content: Spring Security provides **two orthogonal security layers**: **URL-based security** (filter chain) and **method-level security** (AOP proxies). **at-EnableWebSecurity** activates the first layer — it tells Spring to install the **filter chain** that intercepts HTTP requests. This enables: `SecurityFilterChain` beans, request matchers (`requestMatchers("/api/admin/**")`), session management, CSRF protection, and authentication filters. Without `@EnableWebSecurity`, Spring Security is completely inactive — no filters run. **at-EnableMethodSecurity** activates the second layer — it tells Spring to process **method-level annotations** like `@PreAuthorize`, `@PostAuthorize`, and `@Secured`. Spring creates **AOP proxies** around annotated beans and evaluates expressions before/after method invocation. WHY two annotations? Different security concerns. URL-based security is **coarse-grained**: "All users can access /api/public, only ADMIN can access /api/admin." Method-level security is **fine-grained**: "User can view an order only if order.customerId equals user.id." Most production apps use BOTH: URL rules for general access control, method annotations for data-level authorization. IMPORTANT: `@EnableMethodSecurity` replaced `@EnableGlobalMethodSecurity` in Spring Security 6 — the old annotation is deprecated.

sections.title: When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: **Use at-EnableWebSecurity (always required)** for activating Spring Security in any application. It's the master switch. Without it, no security features work — no filter chain, no authentication, no authorization. Use it to configure: URL-based access rules using SecurityFilterChain, session management policies (STATELESS for REST, IF_REQUIRED for web apps), CSRF protection (enable for web forms, disable for REST), custom authentication filters like JWT validation, and exception handling (401 and 403 responses). This is your foundation layer. **Use at-EnableMethodSecurity (optional, for fine-grained control)** when you need authorization decisions at the method level based on dynamic data. Use it for: data-level access control (user can edit ONLY their own posts), complex role checks that go beyond simple URL patterns (hasRole and additional conditions), pre-authorization checks using SpEL (Spring Expression Language) like at-PreAuthorize with principal-dot-userId equals entity-dot-ownerId, post-authorization filtering (at-PostFilter removes items from returned collections the user can't see), and securing service layer methods independent of the controller layer. Common pattern: use URL security to block unauthenticated users at the gateway, use method security to enforce ownership and data-specific rules inside the service layer.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@EnableWebSecurity**: mandatory annotation to activate Spring Security — enables filter chain and SecurityFilterChain configuration
**@EnableMethodSecurity**: optional annotation to activate method-level security — enables @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @Secured annotations
**AOP proxies**: method security works via Spring AOP — annotations are processed through proxies, not direct method calls
**SpEL expressions**: @PreAuthorize supports Spring Expression Language — access principal, method parameters, bean references in authorization logic
**Replaced annotation**: @EnableMethodSecurity replaced @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6 — old annotation is deprecated
**Common mistake**: using @PreAuthorize without @EnableMethodSecurity — annotation is silently ignored, no error thrown
**Layer separation**: URL security (coarse) protects endpoints by role, method security (fine) protects data by ownership or dynamic conditions

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between at-EnableWebSecurity and at-EnableMethodSecurity is about two different layers of security. at-EnableWebSecurity is the master switch. It activates Spring Security's filter chain. Without this annotation, Spring Security is completely inactive. No filters run, no authentication, nothing. When you add at-EnableWebSecurity, Spring installs 10 to 15 filters that intercept every HTTP request. This lets you configure URL-based security rules. You create a SecurityFilterChain bean where you define request matchers, like allowing slash-api-slash-public to everyone or requiring ADMIN role for slash-api-slash-admin. You also configure session management, CSRF settings, and authentication filters here. This is coarse-grained security. You're protecting entire endpoints based on URL patterns and roles. at-EnableMethodSecurity is different. It activates method-level security annotations like at-PreAuthorize, at-PostAuthorize, and at-Secured. This is fine-grained security. You put annotations directly on controller or service methods to enforce authorization rules at the method level. For example, at-PreAuthorize with hasRole ADMIN restricts a method to admins. But the real power is SpEL, Spring Expression Language. You can write complex conditions like at-PreAuthorize with principal-dot-userId equals entity-dot-ownerId. This checks that the logged-in user owns the data they're trying to modify. How does it work? Spring Security uses AOP, aspect-oriented programming, to create proxies around your beans. When a method with at-PreAuthorize is called, the proxy intercepts it, evaluates the expression, and either allows or denies access. If denied, it throws an AccessDeniedException, which triggers your AccessDeniedHandler to return a 403 response. Here's the key difference. URL security happens at the filter level, before your controller runs. Method security happens inside your application, when a method is invoked. URL security is good for general access control: authenticated users can access slash-api-slash-orders, only admins can access slash-api-slash-admin. Method security is good for data-specific rules: user can view ONLY their own orders, not everyone's. One critical mistake freshers make is using at-PreAuthorize without enabling it. If you don't have at-EnableMethodSecurity on a configuration class, at-PreAuthorize annotations are silently ignored. No error, no exception. The method runs without authorization checks. That's a security hole. Always verify method security is enabled if you're using annotations. Another point to mention: at-EnableMethodSecurity replaced at-EnableGlobalMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6. The old annotation is deprecated. If you see tutorials using at-EnableGlobalMethodSecurity, that's outdated. Use at-EnableMethodSecurity instead. In most production applications, you use BOTH annotations. You use at-EnableWebSecurity to set up the filter chain, define URL rules, configure sessions and CSRF. You use at-EnableMethodSecurity to add fine-grained authorization in your service layer. They complement each other. URL security is your first line of defense. Method security is your second, data-level line of defense. To stand out, explain the two-layer architecture. Show you understand that URL security happens in filters, method security happens in AOP proxies. Mention SpEL for dynamic authorization checks. And definitely mention that at-EnableMethodSecurity replaced the old annotation in Spring Security 6. That shows you're up to date with the framework.

speakable_v2.hook: @PreAuthorize silently does nothing without @EnableMethodSecurity — that's a bug that's hard to debug because there's no error message, the annotation is just ignored.

beats.content: @EnableWebSecurity activates Spring Security's filter-based web security — the SecurityFilterChain bean, URL authorization rules, filter chain registration. In Spring Boot it's technically optional because security auto-configuration handles it, but it's standard practice to include it explicitly.

@EnableMethodSecurity activates AOP-based method security — it's what makes @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, and @Secured work. This is NOT auto-configured in Spring Boot. Without it, those annotations are silently ignored. No error, no warning, just no security.

gotcha: in Spring Security 5, you used @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity(prePostEnabled=true) to enable method security. That annotation was replaced by @EnableMethodSecurity in Spring Security 6. If you see the old annotation in a codebase, that's a Spring Boot 2 project.

speakable_v2.cap: @EnableWebSecurity for filter-based security, @EnableMethodSecurity for annotation-based method security. Both often appear together. @EnableMethodSecurity is the one you must add manually — Spring Boot won't add it for you.
followup_handoff: Method security works via Spring AOP proxy — which means it only works on calls through the Spring proxy, not on internal this.method() calls within the same class.
We can also look at the proxyTargetClass behavior and when it matters for method security.
